Reconquista. The centuries-long Christian reconquest of the Iberian Peninsula from Muslim rule, spanning roughly from the eighth century after the Umayyad conquest to fourteen ninety-two when the final Islamic Sultanate of Granada fell to the Christian Catholic Monarchs. It fundamentally reshaped medieval Europe, driving the development of Christian kingdoms in northern Iberia and culminating in the emergence of Spain as a major European power.

The Reconquista began in earnest after the eighth-century Umayyad conquest of Iberia left most of the peninsula under Islamic control. Christian kingdoms persisted in the north: Asturias, Leon, Castile, Aragon, Portugal. Al-Andalus, the Islamic civilization in Iberia, was culturally sophisticated and religiously pluralistic, though non-Muslims faced dhimmi status. Its libraries, scholars, and architecture influenced medieval Europe profoundly.

The Battle of Tours in seven thirty-two in what is now France, though not technically Iberian, marked the symbolic limit of Islamic expansion northward and energized Christian resistance mythology. Progress was fitful. The Reconquista advanced and retreated over centuries. The Taifa period in the eleventh century saw Islamic Iberia fragment into petty kingdoms, enabling Christian advances. Subsequent waves of North African Muslim invaders—the Almoravids and Almohads—reversed some gains.

The Catholic Monarchs Isabella and Ferdinand unified Castile and Aragon through marriage and orchestrated the final siege of Granada from fourteen eighty-two to fourteen ninety-two, expelling the last Muslim rulers and establishing Christian supremacy. The Reconquista was intertwined with the Crusades ideologically. It was framed as holy war against Islam and fueled anti-Islamic sentiment that persisted into the modern era. After fourteen ninety-two, the monarchs expelled Jews and Muslims who refused conversion, and the Spanish Inquisition targeted converts, marking a violent end to medieval pluralism in Iberia. It connects to the Crusades, which the Reconquista shared with the crusading ideal of recovering Christian lands from Muslim rule, to Al-Andalus, the Islamic civilization that dominated most of medieval Iberia and shaped Christian Europe through its scholarship and culture, to Spain, which the Reconquista created through unified Christian kingdoms that became the Spanish nation, to Medieval Europe, where the Reconquista was a defining conflict of medieval Christian Europe and influenced its religious and political identity, and to Islam, whose Iberian civilization was sophisticated and whose fall marked the end of a pluralistic medieval Mediterranean.
